extraction_notes.note: The paper's own bootstrapping cycle: helpful bounds (Part 5) use the FFN-drift lemma, which uses the convergence theorem, which uses kernel perturbation, which uses the helpful bounds; the paper closes it by a stopping-time argument (Remark H.7).
evidence: the last step follows from Part 6 and Part 13 of Lemma~\ref{lem:helpful_bounds}
From Lemma~\ref{lem:perturbations} we have (with probability at least $1-\delta$), with the $1/n$ factor from Part~15:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:ffn_drift}, $\|A_{(\nu)}(t) - A_{(\nu)}(0)\|_F \le R_A := O(1/(\sqrt m\,\omega\lambda N))$.
We emphasize the {\it bootstrapping cycle} between Lemma~\ref{lem:helpful_bounds} (Part~5), Lemma~\ref{lem:ffn_drift}, and Theorem~\ref{thm:convergence}

extraction_notes.note: The source keeps both branches of \ifdefined 1 ... \else ... \fi, so displays such as (eq:F) and (eq:ODE_update) appear twice and are numbered twice; each is one node with the other copy in also_stated_at, and the duplicated Related Work section got no nodes.

Main-text results are informal versions of appendix results with their own proof sketches. Rule 'proof sketch -> rigor semi_formal, alternative proves edge' conflicts with 'no rigor on proofs' and with alternative needing a main proof of the same node, so the informal results and their sketches are separate nodes, the sketch gets a plain proves edge and no rigor, and each formal result gets a uses edge into the sketch.

The long appendix proofs are split at the authors' 'Proof of Part N' and bold headings (not detected as labels by the parser); long parts were given child steps only where author sub-labels (Step 1/2/3, Base case) occur.
Remark H.7 contains the stopping-time argument that closes the bootstrapping cycle; kept as remark (the author's word) rather than a proof, since it proves no single stated result.

Experimental sections (7, D), related work, and discussion paragraphs (e.g. Discussion of Thm 6.1, the generic vs transformer ingredient lists of C.2, the matching-sense paragraphs of C.3) were not made nodes beyond a few remarks and open problems.

nodes.name: Index set [d]
also_stated_at: For any positive integer $n$, we use $[n]$ to denote set $\{1,2,\cdots,n\}$.

nodes.name: l_p-norm
nodes.statement: For $u \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the $\ell_p$-norm is $\|u\|_p := ( \sum_{k=1}^d |u_k|^p )^{1/p}$.

nodes.name: Frobenius norm
nodes.statement: The Frobenius norm of $U \in \mathbb{R}^{d_1 \times d_2}$ is $\|U\|_F := ( \sum_{(k_1, k_2) \in [d_1] \times [d_2]} U_{k_1, k_2}^2 )^{1/2}$.
also_stated_at: We denote the Frobenius norm as  $\|A\|_F:=( \sum_{i\in [n], j\in [d]} A_{i,j}^2 )^{1/2}$.

nodes.name: Smallest eigenvalue
nodes.statement: For a matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$, $\lambda_{\min}(A)$ denotes its smallest eigenvalue.
also_stated_at: We define $\lambda_{\min}(\cdot)$ as a function that outputs the minimum eigenvalues of the input matrix, e.g. matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ has eigenvalues $\{ \lambda_1, \lambda_2, \cdots, \lambda_n \}$, $\lambda_{\min}(A) = \min \{ \lambda_1, \lambda_2, \cdots, \lambda_n \}$.

nodes.name: Indicator function
nodes.statement: The indicator function $\mathbb{I}\{E_1, \dots, E_n\}$ equals $1$ if all events $E_1, \dots, E_n$ occur, and $0$ otherwise.
also_stated_at: We use $\mathbb{I}\{{\sf E}_1, {\sf E}_2, \cdots, {\sf E}_n\}$ to denote the indicator for event set $\{{\sf E}_1, {\sf E}_2, \cdots, {\sf E}_n\}$, only when ${\sf E}_1, {\sf E}_2, \cdots, {\sf E}_n$ are all true, $\mathbb{I}\{{\sf E}_1, {\sf E}_2, \cdots, {\sf E}_n\} = 1$; otherwise, it equals to $0$.

nodes.name: Reshaping map mat
nodes.statement: The mapping $\mathrm{mat}: \mathbb{R}^{d^2} \to \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ reshapes a vector $a$ into a matrix such that $\mathrm{mat}_{k_1, k_2}(a) = a_{(k_1-1)d + k_2}$ for $(k_1, k_2) \in [d] \times [d]$.
also_stated_at: For a vector $a \in \mathbb{R}^{d^2}$, function $\mathrm{mat}$ reshapes $a$ to a $d \times d$ matrix, where its $(i, j)$-th entry is $\mathrm{mat}_{i, j}(a) = a_{(i-1)d+j}$ for $(i, j) \in [d] \times [d]$.

nodes.name: Row-major flattening vec
nodes.statement: Conversely, $\mathrm{vec}: \mathbb{R}^{n \times d} \to \mathbb{R}^{nd}$ flattens a matrix $A$ into a vector with $\mathrm{vec}_k(A) = A_{\lceil k/d\rceil,\,k - (\lceil k/d\rceil-1)d}$ for $k \in [nd]$, so that $\mathrm{vec}$ is the {\it row-major} flattening that is the inverse of $\mathrm{mat}$ (in particular $\mathrm{mat}_{k_1, k_2}(\mathrm{vec}(A)) = A_{k_1, k_2}$).
also_stated_at: For a matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$, function $\mathrm{vec}$ flattens $A$ to an $nd$-dimensional vector (row-major) where its $i$-th entry is $\mathrm{vec}_i(A) = A_{\lceil i/d\rceil,\,i - (\lceil i/d\rceil - 1)d}$ for $i \in [nd]$, so $\mathrm{vec} = \mathrm{mat}^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Entry notation for matrix-valued functions
nodes.statement: For a function $f: X \to \mathbb{R}^{d_1 \times d_2}$, $f_{k_1, k_2}(x)$ denotes the $(k_1, k_2)$-entry of $f(x)$.

nodes.name: Standard basis vector
nodes.statement: $e_k \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is the standard basis vector with a $1$ in the $k$-th entry and $0$ elsewhere.

nodes.name: Sequence-to-sequence regression task (input space and target function)
nodes.statement: We consider a sequence-to-sequence regression task with an input space ${\cal X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{L \times d}$ as the space of encoded input sequence\footnote{We choose the max length of sequence $L$ considerably large, for sequences with a length less than $L$, we use padding to fill them.}, and noiseless target outputs $F^*(X)\in[C_{\rm lower}, C_{\rm upper}]^{L\times d}$ bounded by constants $C_{\rm lower}, C_{\rm upper}\in\mathbb{R}$, where $F^*: {\cal X} \to \mathbb{R}^{L\times d}$ is the optimal measurable function with minimum risk.
nodes.statement_short: Inputs live in ${\cal X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{L\times d}$; the noiseless target $F^*$ is bounded entrywise.

nodes.name: Noisy targets
nodes.statement: The noisy targets is given by $Y=F^*(X)+\Xi\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d}$, where $\Xi\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d}$ is the noise matrix.

nodes.name: Data distribution and model function
nodes.statement: Given a model class ${\cal F}$, the data distribution is ${\cal D} = \{(X, F^*(X)+\Xi)\} \subset {\cal X} \times \mathbb{R}^{L\times d}$ and model function $F \in {\cal F}$.

nodes.name: Expected risk and excess risk
Training dataset
nodes.statement: Besides, we have an accessible dataset $\mathbb{D} = \{(X_i, Y_i)\}_{i=1}^n \subset {\cal D}$ where each data point is independently sampled from ${\cal D}$.

nodes.name: Sub-Gaussian noise condition
nodes.statement: We discuss two noise condition in this paper: i) the random noise $\Xi \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times d}$ is centred by ${\bf 0}_{L \times d}$ and is {\it sub-Gaussian} with variance proxy $\max_{\ell \in [L], k \in [d]} \|\Xi_{\ell, k}\|_{\psi_2}^2 \le \xi^2$ (so that ${\mathbb{E}}[\Xi]=0$ and ${\mathbb{E}}[\exp(t\Xi_{\ell,k})]\le \exp(t^2\xi^2/2)$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$); ii) the Gaussian case $\Xi_{\ell,k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\xi^2)$ used in the statistical lower bound (Theorem~\ref{thm:lower_stat}) is a special case.
nodes.statement_short: Noise is centred sub-Gaussian with variance proxy $\xi^2$; the Gaussian case is used for the statistical lower bound.

nodes.name: Unit-scale tokens (RMS normalization)
nodes.statement: For any input matrix $X \sim {\cal X} $, $\| X_\ell \|_2 = \Theta(1)$ holds for each token vector $\ell \in [L]$ due to the utilization of RMS normalization \citep{zs19} after the embedding layer.

nodes.name: N-layer transformer model
nodes.statement_short: The model is an $\varepsilon$-scaled composition of $N$ transformer blocks applied to $X+E$.

nodes.name: Transformer model function
nodes.statement: F(X, \theta) := \varepsilon \cdot F_{(N)}(F_{(N-1)}( \cdots F_{(2)}(F_{(1)}(X + E, \theta), \theta) \cdots ), \theta),
nodes.label: eq:F

nodes.name: Scaling coefficient epsilon
nodes.statement: $\varepsilon > 0$ is the scaling coefficient to control the norm of the initial parameters, which helps to reduce the model complexity in the analysis.

Unbiased minibatch

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement: Although the derivation of the gradient is complicated, the technique used for the proof is just the chain rule. We provide the complete proof in Appendix~\ref{app:proof_learning_dynamics}.

nodes.name: Layer-wise positive definiteness of the initial NTK
nodes.statement:
Define $H_{(
u)}'(0) \in \mathbb{R}^{nL 	imes nL}$ with $(p,q)$-entry $\langle  eta_{(
u),p}(0), eta_{(
u),q}(0)angle$. We assume $ rac{1}{\omega}H_{(

u\in[N]$, with $\lambda_{(

u\in[N]}\lambda_{(

nodes.statement_short: Each layer's initial FFN kernel $H'_{(\nu)}(0)/\omega$ is positive definite, with worst-case spectral gap $\lambda>0$.
nodes.label: ass:positive_definite

nodes.name: PD assumption follows from input non-degeneracy
nodes.statement:
The kernel $H_{(
u)}'(0)$ is the standard 2-layer ReLU NTK over the layer-$
u$ attention outputs $\{o_{(
u),p}(0)\}_{p\in[nL]}$, so positive definiteness reduces to a non-degeneracy condition on those outputs (no two normalized vectors parallel) by the same argument as \citep{dzps19, dllw19, os20}. We give a sufficient condition together with its proof in Appendix~ef{app_sub:pd_sufficient} (Lemma~ef{lem:pd_sufficient}); the condition is automatically satisfied under RMS normalization and Gaussian initialization (Remark~ef{rem:p2_non_parallel}), so Assumption~ef{ass:positive_definite} is a consequence of input non-degeneracy and the architecture rather than an opaque ansatz.
nodes.statement_short: Assumption 5.1 reduces to non-parallel attention outputs, which RMSNorm plus Gaussian initialization provide.

nodes.name: Good Properties and Good Model Class
nodes.statement: Fix dataset size $n$. We say model $F(X,\theta)$ has Good Properties if, with a considerably small constant $C>0$ and $B := \max\{O(\sqrt{\log(Nmd/\delta)}), 1\}$: \begin{multicols}{3} \begin{enumerate} \item $\omega = \Theta(\frac{1}{N L^2d^{2.5}B^3})$; \item $\kappa = \frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}$; \item $m = \Omega(\frac{n^3L^5\exp(Cd)}{\omega^6\lambda^6\delta^3 N^{2}})$. \end{enumerate} \end{multicols} The Good Model Class is ${\cal F}_{\sf M, T, N}(\mathbb{D}):= \{F(\cdot, \theta({\sf T})) : \theta(0) \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_{\sf M}), \theta({\sf T}) \in {\cal A}_{{\sf T},{\sf N}}(\theta(0), \mathbb{D})\}$ with $|\mathbb{D}|={\sf N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Width, output and attention scalings ($\omega$, $\kappa=1/\sqrt m$, $m$ large) for lazy training; the Good Model Class is all gradient-flow endpoints.
nodes.label: def:gd

nodes.name: Comments on the Good Properties scalings
nodes.statement: While the scaling requirements in Definition~\ref{def:gd} may appear distinct from standard heuristic initializations, they serve as essential theoretical proxies for ensuring stability in the NTK regime. Specifically, the choice of $\omega$ mirrors the {\it zero-output} or {\it small-norm initialization} assumptions common in deep learning theory and in training super-deep transformers~\citep{bmm+21, zdm19, wmd+22}, effectively mitigating the residual branch's impact to guarantee a minimum input norm for each layer. Furthermore, regarding the model width $m$, we highlight the inverse dependence on depth ($m \propto N^{-2}$): this relationship suggests a trade-off where deeper architectures alleviate the strict lower bound on width, implying that the total parameter capacity can be distributed toward depth without requiring an exponentially prohibitive width (extended discussion in Appendix~\ref{app_sub:practitioner}). Finally, the attention scaling $\kappa = 1/\sqrt{m}$ (in place of the conventional $1/\sqrt{d_{\rm head}}$) plays the same stabilizing role for the attention kernel: it is the unique choice that keeps the kernel feature norm $\|\gamma_{(\nu),p}(t)\|_2 = o(1/\sqrt m)$ (Part~16 of Lemma~\ref{lem:helpful_bounds}) in our width regime $m = \Omega(\mathrm{poly}({\sf N}))$. The two conventions coincide up to a constant for a single-head attention layer with $m=\Theta(d)$; the architectural implications of this convention are discussed in Appendix~\ref{app_sub:U_parameterization}.
nodes.statement_short: The $\omega$, $m$ and $\kappa$ choices act as small-norm initialization and NTK-stability proxies; $\kappa=1/\sqrt m$ keeps $\|\gamma\|_2=o(1/\sqrt m)$.

nodes.name: Kernel perturbation and loss decay (informal)
nodes.statement: Under Assumption~\ref{ass:positive_definite} and Definition~\ref{def:gd}, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over $\theta(0)$, the kernel perturbation and loss-decay bound are: \begin{align*} \lambda_{\min}(H_{(\nu)}(t)) \ge \omega\lambda/2,\qquad {\mathbb{E}}\big[\tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t}{\cal L}(t,\mathbb{D})\big] \le -\frac{C\cdot\omega\lambda N\cdot \varepsilon^2}{\mathsf{N}}\cdot {\cal L}(t,\mathbb{D}). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: With high probability the layer kernels stay above $\omega\lambda/2$ and the loss decays at rate $C\omega\lambda N\varepsilon^2/{\sf N}$.
assumptions: Under Assumption~\ref{ass:positive_definite} and Definition~\ref{def:gd}
with probability at least $1-\delta$ over $\theta(0)$
nodes.label: lem:perturbations:informal

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Lemma 5.3
nodes.statement: The stability of the PD property is ensured by $\lambda_{\min}(H') \ge \lambda_{\min}(H) - \| H - H' \|_F$ (Fact~\ref{fac:lambda_min_perturb}), since the perturbation $\| H - H' \|_F$ remains considerably small throughout training. The upper bound on the perturbation converges due to the increasing feed-forward layer width $m$ and the decreasing weight perturbation radius $R$, leading to the {\it Lazy Learning} regime. The complete proof of this lemma is stated in Appendix~\ref{app:proof_lperturbations}.
nodes.statement_short: Weyl-type eigenvalue perturbation plus a small weight-drift radius from wide FFNs keeps the kernel PD (lazy regime).

nodes.name: Factors of scaling law (M, N, T, C)
nodes.statement: We define: \begin{multicols}{2} \begin{itemize} \item Model Size: ${\sf M} := O(Nmd)$. \item Dataset Size: ${\sf N} := n$. \item Training Time: ${\sf T} := T$. \item Total Compute: ${\sf C} := O({\sf MT}|\mathbb{B}|) \le O({\sf MTN})$. \end{itemize} \end{multicols}
nodes.statement_short: Model size $O(Nmd)$, dataset size $n$, training time $T$, compute $O({\sf MT}|\mathbb{B}|)$.
nodes.label: def:factors

nodes.name: Training convergence (informal)
nodes.statement: Let Definitions~\ref{def:gd},~\ref{def:factors} and Assumption~\ref{ass:positive_definite} hold, $\delta\in(0, 0.1)$, and $\alpha_{\rm cr}:=C\cdot\omega\lambda N$ with $\omega N=\Theta(1/(L^2 d^{2.5}B^3))$. With probability at least $1-\delta$, \begin{align*} {\cal L}({\sf T},\mathbb{D}) \le \exp\!\left(-\alpha_{\rm cr}\cdot \frac{\varepsilon^2\, {\sf T}}{\mathsf{N}}\right)\cdot {\cal L}(0,\mathbb{D}),\quad \forall F\in{\cal F}_{\sf M,T,N}(\mathbb{D}). \end{align*} Equivalently, absorbing $\omega N=\mathrm{poly}(1/L,1/d,1/B)$ into $\bar\alpha:=\mathrm{poly}(L,d,B,\lambda)$, we have ${\cal L}({\sf T})\le \exp(-\bar\alpha\,\varepsilon^2{\sf T}/\mathsf{N})\cdot{\cal L}(0, \mathbb{D})$. The $1/\mathsf{N}$ factor traces to the average-loss convention ${\cal L} = \frac{1}{n}\|{\sf F}-{\sf Y}\|_F^2$ and is essential to the scaling law; see Remark~\ref{rem:n_in_rate}.
nodes.statement_short: Training loss decays as $\exp(-\alpha_{\rm cr}\varepsilon^2{\sf T}/{\sf N})$ for every model in the Good Model Class.
assumptions: Let Definitions~\ref{def:gd},~\ref{def:factors} and Assumption~\ref{ass:positive_definite} hold, $\delta\in(0, 0.1)$
conclusions: {\cal L}({\sf T},\mathbb{D}) \le \exp\!\left(-\alpha_{\rm cr}\cdot \frac{\varepsilon^2\, {\sf T}}{\mathsf{N}}\right)\cdot {\cal L}(0,\mathbb{D}),\quad \forall F\in{\cal F}_{\sf M,T,N}(\mathbb{D}).
nodes.label: thm:convergence:informal

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Theorem 5.5
nodes.statement: We first connect the hidden-state gradient norm to the training objective (Part~15 of Lemma~\ref{lem:helpful_bounds}) and combine it with the kernel-stability bound of Lemma~\ref{lem:perturbations:informal}; the model convergence therefore benefits exponentially from the model size (neural depth and width) and the training time. The discretization to SGD via a Taylor expansion follows the standard route of \citep{dzps19} and \citep{lssy25}, recorded in Appendix~\ref{app_sub:discrete_sgd}; the detailed proof is in Appendix~\ref{app_sub:convergence}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the gradient-norm/loss relation with kernel stability; discretization follows the standard SGD route.

nodes.name: Approximation bound (informal)
nodes.statement: Under Assumption~\ref{ass:positive_definite} and Definition~\ref{def:gd}, choosing $\varepsilon\lesssim {\sf M}^{-1}$, with probability at least $1-\delta$, \begin{align*} \lim_{{\sf T}\to+\infty}\inf_{F\in{\cal F}_{\sf M,T,N}(\mathbb{D})}{\mathbb{E}}_{(X,Y)\sim \mathcal{D}}\big[\|F(X)-F^*(X)\|_F^2\big] \le {\sf M}^{-2}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: With $\varepsilon\lesssim{\sf M}^{-1}$, the best trained model approximates $F^*$ to squared error ${\sf M}^{-2}$.
assumptions: Under Assumption~\ref{ass:positive_definite} and Definition~\ref{def:gd}
choosing $\varepsilon\lesssim {\sf M}^{-1}$
nodes.label: cor:approximation:informal

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Corollary 5.6
nodes.statement: According to the conditions on the target function $F^*$ in Section~\ref{sec:preli}, we formulate its expression in the RKHS; the approximation error is then bounded by a considerably small $\varepsilon$ together with the over-parameterized width $m$, similarly to Theorem 3.2 in \citep{adh+19}. The formal proof is in Appendix~\ref{app_sub:approximation}.
nodes.statement_short: Express $F^*$ in the RKHS and bound the error via small $\varepsilon$ and wide FFNs, as in Arora et al.'s Theorem 3.2.

nodes.name: Generalization bound of the ERM (informal)
nodes.statement: Under the conditions of Corollary~\ref{cor:approximation:informal} and $\varepsilon=\Theta(1/{\sf M})$, define ${\cal F}_{\sf M, N}(\mathbb{D}) := \{F(\cdot,\theta) : \theta\in\mathbb{R}^{\sf M}\}$ (the ERM class over the full parameter space). With probability at least $1-\delta$, \begin{align*} \inf_{F\in{\cal F}_{\sf M,N}(\mathbb{D})}\sup_{\mathbb{D}\in{\cal D}}\Delta{\cal R}(F) \le \big(4{\sf M}^{-1}+Ld\cdot \xi\big)\cdot {\sf M}^{-1}+\frac{Ld\cdot \xi^2}{\sf N}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: The transformer ERM has excess risk at most $(4{\sf M}^{-1}+Ld\xi){\sf M}^{-1}+Ld\xi^2/{\sf N}$.
assumptions: Under the conditions of Corollary~\ref{cor:approximation:informal} and $\varepsilon=\Theta(1/{\sf M})$
conclusions: \inf_{F\in{\cal F}_{\sf M,N}(\mathbb{D})}\sup_{\mathbb{D}\in{\cal D}}\Delta{\cal R}(F) \le \big(4{\sf M}^{-1}+Ld\cdot \xi\big)\cdot {\sf M}^{-1}+\frac{Ld\cdot \xi^2}{\sf N}.
nodes.label: thm:generalization:informal

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Theorem 5.7
nodes.statement: The proof combines Lemma 11 of \citep{sch17} for the generalization error with Corollary~\ref{cor:approximation:informal} for the approximation error. The full proof is shown in Appendix~\ref{app_sub:erm}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Schmidt-Hieber's ERM generalization lemma with the approximation corollary.

nodes.name: Two-stage scaling law (informal)
nodes.statement: Let all pre-conditions hold as Corollary~\ref{cor:approximation:informal} and choose $\varepsilon = \Theta(\xi/{\sf N})$. Then, with probability at least $1-\delta$, the following condition divides the scaling trend into two stages: \begin{align} {\sf C} > \frac{{\sf N}^7\log({\sf N}\cdot Ld/\xi^2)}{\xi^2}. \end{align} \begin{itemize} \item {\it Stage I: Compute-Starved Stage.} If Eq.~\eqref{eq:cond_C} does not hold, the excess risk admits the two-sided bound \begin{align*} c'\cdot e^{-C_{\rm opt}\sqrt{\kappa}\,\xi^2{\sf C}/{\sf N}^7}\cdot{\cal L}(0,\mathbb{D})\;\le\;\inf_{{\cal F}_{\sf M, T, N}(\mathbb{D})}\sup_{\mathbb{D}\in{\cal D}}\Delta{\cal R}(F)\;\le\;C\cdot e^{-\alpha\,\xi^2{\sf C}/{\sf N}^7}\cdot{\cal L}(0,\mathbb{D}), \end{align*} where $c', C_{\rm opt}, C, \alpha = \mathrm{poly}(L,d,1/\lambda,1/\omega)$ and $\kappa:=\lambda_{\max}/\lambda\le\mathrm{poly}(L,d,1/\delta)$ is the condition number of the initial kernel: the two exponents agree up to a $\sqrt{\kappa}$ factor. \item {\it Stage II: Data-Limited Stage.} If Eq.~\eqref{eq:cond_C} holds, the excess risk follows the matching (up to constants and logarithms) power law \begin{align*} \xi^{12/7}\cdot\widetilde{\Omega}({\sf C}^{-1/7})\;\le\;\inf_{{\cal F}_{\sf M, T, N}(\mathbb{D})}\sup_{\mathbb{D}\in{\cal D}}\Delta{\cal R}(F)\;\le\;\xi^{12/7}\cdot O\left(\frac{{\sf C}}{W({\sf C}/\xi^{12})}\right)^{-1/7}\le\;\xi^{12/7}\cdot\widetilde{O}({\sf C}^{-1/7}), \end{align*} where $W(\cdot)$ is the Lambert $W$ function and $\widetilde{O}, \widetilde{\Omega}$ hide $\log({\sf C})$ factors. \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 6.1 General Scaling Law with Pattern Transition
nodes.statement_short: Excess risk decays exponentially in ${\sf C}/{\sf N}^7$ below a compute threshold and as $\xi^{12/7}{\sf C}^{-1/7}$ above it, with matching lower bounds.
assumptions: Let all pre-conditions hold as Corollary~\ref{cor:approximation:informal} and choose $\varepsilon = \Theta(\xi/{\sf N})$
conclusions: {\it Stage I: Compute-Starved Stage.} If Eq.~\eqref{eq:cond_C} does not hold, the excess risk admits the two-sided bound \begin{align*} c'\cdot e^{-C_{\rm opt}\sqrt{\kappa}\,\xi^2{\sf C}/{\sf N}^7}\cdot{\cal L}(0,\mathbb{D})\;\le\;\inf_{{\cal F}_{\sf M, T, N}(\mathbb{D})}\sup_{\mathbb{D}\in{\cal D}}\Delta{\cal R}(F)\;\le\;C\cdot e^{-\alpha\,\xi^2{\sf C}/{\sf N}^7}\cdot{\cal L}(0,\mathbb{D}), \end{align*}

{\it Stage II: Data-Limited Stage.} If Eq.~\eqref{eq:cond_C} holds, the excess risk follows the matching (up to constants and logarithms) power law \begin{align*} \xi^{12/7}\cdot\widetilde{\Omega}({\sf C}^{-1/7})\;\le\;\inf_{{\cal F}_{\sf M, T, N}(\mathbb{D})}\sup_{\mathbb{D}\in{\cal D}}\Delta{\cal R}(F)\;\le\;\xi^{12/7}\cdot O\left(\frac{{\sf C}}{W({\sf C}/\xi^{12})}\right)^{-1/7}\le\;\xi^{12/7}\cdot\widetilde{O}({\sf C}^{-1/7}), \end{align*}
nodes.label: thm:scaling_law:informal

nodes.name: Stage I/II compute threshold
nodes.statement: {\sf C} > \frac{{\sf N}^7\log({\sf N}\cdot Ld/\xi^2)}{\xi^2}.
nodes.section: 6.1 General Scaling Law with Pattern Transition
nodes.label: eq:cond_C

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Theorem 6.1
nodes.statement: We decompose the excess risk $\Delta{\cal R}(F)$ into three terms: {\it i)} optimization risk ${\cal R}_{\rm optimization} := \| F(\cdot, \theta(t)) - F(\cdot, \theta(\infty)) \|_{L^F({\cal X})}^2$; {\it ii)} approximation risk ${\cal R}_{\rm approximation} := \big\| F(\cdot, \theta(\infty)) - {\rm arg}\inf_{F' \in {\cal F}_{\sf M, \infty, N}} \|F' - F^*\|_{L^F({\cal X})}^2 \big\|_{L^F({\cal X})}^2$; and {\it iii)} estimation risk ${\cal R}_{\rm estimation} := \inf_{F' \in {\cal F}_{\sf M, \infty, N}} \|F' - F^*\|_{L^F({\cal X})}^2$. The second and the third terms are already bounded in Theorem~\ref{thm:generalization:informal}, and the first term relates to the training loss; we thereby utilize Theorem~\ref{thm:convergence:informal} to finish the proof of the upper bounds. The matching lower bounds follow from a Le~Cam two-point reduction in the RKHS (Theorem~\ref{thm:lower_stat:informal}) and a first-order oracle complexity argument (Theorem~\ref{thm:lower_opt:informal}). The formal analysis is stated in Appendix~\ref{app_sub:scaling_law}, the lower bounds in Appendix~\ref{app_sub:lower_bounds}, and the precise sense of ``matching'' in Appendix~\ref{app_sub:matching_precise}.
nodes.section: 6.1 General Scaling Law with Pattern Transition
nodes.statement_short: Split excess risk into optimization, approximation and estimation terms; bound them by the convergence and ERM theorems, with lower bounds from Le Cam and oracle complexity.

nodes.name: Single-variable scaling laws (informal)
nodes.statement: Let all pre-conditions hold as Corollary~\ref{cor:approximation:informal}. Then, with probability at least $1 - \delta$, there exists: \begin{itemize} \item {\bf Time-Law.} We fix the dataset size ${\sf N}$ and model size ${\sf M} = \Omega({\sf N}^3)$, and choosing $\varepsilon = \xi/{\sf N}$, we have $\inf_{{\cal F}_{\sf M, T, N}(\mathbb{D})} \sup_{\mathbb{D} \in {\cal D}} \Delta{\cal R}(F) \leq \exp(-\alpha\,\xi^2\,{\sf T}/{\sf N}^3) + O(\frac{\xi^2}{{\sf N}})$, where the ${\sf N}^3$ in the exponent combines the ${\sf N}^2$ from $\varepsilon=\xi/{\sf N}$ with the $1/{\sf N}$ factor in the convergence rate (Remark~\ref{rem:n_in_rate}). \item {\bf Data-Law.} For any dataset size ${\sf N}$, we let $\varepsilon = \xi/{\sf N}$, ${\sf M} = \Omega({\sf N}^3)$ and ${\sf T} = \widetilde{\Omega}(\frac{{\sf N}^3}{\xi^2})$, we have: $\inf_{{\cal F}_{\sf M, T, N}(\mathbb{D})} \sup_{\mathbb{D} \in {\cal D}} \Delta{\cal R}(F) \leq O(\frac{\xi^2}{{\sf N}})$. \item {\bf Model-Law.} We fix the dataset size ${\sf N}$ and let training time ${\sf T} = \widetilde{\Omega}(\frac{{\sf M}^{2\zeta}{\sf N}}{\xi^2})$, where $\zeta \in (0, 1/3]$. Choosing $\varepsilon = \xi/{\sf M}^{\zeta}$, before the model size ${\sf M}$ is greater than ${\sf N}^{1/\zeta}$, we have $\inf_{{\cal F}_{\sf M, T, N}(\mathbb{D})} \sup_{\mathbb{D} \in {\cal D}} \Delta{\cal R}(F) \leq \xi^2 {\sf M}^{-\zeta}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 6.1 General Scaling Law with Pattern Transition
nodes.statement_short: Fixing two of (${\sf T},{\sf N},{\sf M}$) gives a time law, a data law $O(\xi^2/{\sf N})$ and a model law $\xi^2{\sf M}^{-\zeta}$.
assumptions: Let all pre-conditions hold as Corollary~\ref{cor:approximation:informal}
nodes.label: thm:single_law:informal

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Theorem 6.2
nodes.statement: This theorem is derived from the intermediate results of Theorem~\ref{thm:scaling_law:informal}: for the three variables ${\sf T}$, ${\sf M}$, and ${\sf N}$, we fix two of them to get the single law of the remaining one. The complete derivation is in Appendix~\ref{app_sub:scaling_law}.
nodes.section: 6.1 General Scaling Law with Pattern Transition
nodes.statement_short: Fix two of the three variables in the intermediate bounds of the two-stage law.

nodes.name: Data-size-dependent noise level
nodes.statement: However, there exists a possibility that including more data leads to the noise level $\xi$ growing with the dataset size, which we denote as $\xi({\sf N})$.

nodes.name: Noise-driven breakdown of the data scaling law
nodes.statement: When $\xi({\sf N}) \propto {\sf N}^{1/2}$ (or, in terms of compute, $\xi \propto {\sf C}^{1/12}$), the upper bound on the excess risk degrades to $O(1)$, effectively nullifying the data scaling law.
nodes.statement_short: If the noise level grows like ${\sf N}^{1/2}$, the excess-risk bound degrades to $O(1)$ and data scaling fails.
assumptions: $\xi({\sf N}) \propto {\sf N}^{1/2}$
conclusions: the upper bound on the excess risk degrades to $O(1)$, effectively nullifying the data scaling law

nodes.name: Causality-induced matrix-to-vector reduction
nodes.statement:
Concretely, the matrix-form gradient flow $ rac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t}\mathsf{F}(t)$ on $\mathsf{F}\in\mathbb{R}^{nL	imes d}$ becomes the vector form
\[
 rac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t}\mu_{(
u)}(t) = -\,(H_{(
u)}(t)\otimes I_d)\cdot 
abla_{\mu_{(
u)}}\mathcal{L}(t,\mathbb{D}),\qquad \mu_{(
u)}(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{nL	imes d},
\]
where the Kronecker structure $H_{(
u)}\otimes I_d$ on the $nL$ vector samples replaces what would otherwise be a 4-tensor on $\mathbb{R}^{L	imes d}	imes\mathbb{R}^{L	imes d}$.
nodes.statement_short: Under the causal mask, the matrix gradient flow becomes a vector flow driven by $H_{(\nu)}\otimes I_d$ on $nL$ token samples.

nodes.name: FFN drift control under trainable A (informal)
nodes.statement:
Let $A_{(
u)}(t)$ evolve by gradient flow as in Equation~\eqref{eq:ODE_update}. Under Definition~ef{def:gd} with the strengthened width $m = \Omega ig( rac{n^4 L^6 d^2 \exp(Cd)}{\omega^6 \lambda^8 \delta^4 N^4} ig)$, with probability at least $1-\delta$:  egin{align*} \max_{
u\in[N]}\|A_{(
u)}(t) - A_{(
u)}(0)\|_F \leq O\Big( rac{1}{\sqrt{m}\,\omega\lambda N}\Big), \end{align*} and the layer-aggregated tangent kernel still satisfies $\lambda_{\min}(H_{(
u)}(t)\otimes I_d) \ge \omega\lambda/4$ uniformly in $t\ge 0$. In particular, every conclusion of Theorem~ef{thm:convergence:informal} and Theorem~ef{thm:generalization:informal} continues to hold, with the constants on the RHS replaced by absolute constants that absorb the new contribution of the FFN tangent feature.
nodes.statement_short: Under a strengthened width, the trained FFN read-out drifts by $O(1/(\sqrt m\omega\lambda N))$ and the kernel stays above $\omega\lambda/4$.
assumptions: Let $A_{(\nu)}(t)$ evolve by gradient flow as in Equation~\eqref{eq:ODE_update}
conclusions: and the layer-aggregated tangent kernel still satisfies $\lambda_{\min}(H_{(\nu)}(t)\otimes I_d) \ge \omega\lambda/4$ uniformly in $t\ge 0$
nodes.label: lem:ffn_drift:informal

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Lemma B.1
nodes.statement:
The post-activation FFN feature $\Lambda_{(
u),i,\ell}^{m ffn}(t) := (\omega/\sqrt m)\,{m ReLU}(\mathrm{Softmax}(\cdots)$ $ X W_{(
u)}(t)) \in \mathbb{R}^{1	imes m}$ has bounded norm by Parts~3 and~5 of Lemma~ef{lem:helpful_bounds}. The gradient of the loss with respect to $A_{(
u)}$ is therefore controlled by the same $\varepsilon\sqrt{{\cal L}(t,\mathbb{D})}$ envelope as that of $W_{(
u)}$. Repeating the bootstrapping step of Lemma~ef{lem:perturbations:informal} with the additional kernel feature $\alpha_{(
u),p}(t):= \Lambda^{m ffn}_{(
u),p}(t)$ adds an $O(\omega)$ contribution to the kernel perturbation; the strengthened width condition is precisely what is needed for this contribution to remain $\le \omega\lambda/4$ at all times. The full proof appears in Appendix~ef{app:proof_lperturbations}.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the FFN feature norm, hence the $A$-gradient, and repeat the kernel-perturbation bootstrap with the extra feature.

nodes.name: Statistical lower bound (informal)
nodes.statement: Fix a non-trivial subspace ${\cal H}^*\subseteq{\cal H}_K$ of the RKHS associated with the layer-wise NTKs. There exists a family of target functions $\{F_\theta^*\}_{\theta\in\Theta_{\sf N}}\subset {\cal H}^*$ and a constant $c>0$ such that for any (possibly randomized) estimator $\widehat F$ measurable with respect to $\mathbb{D}\sim {\cal D}^{\otimes {\sf N}}$: \begin{align*} \sup_{F^*\in\{F_\theta^*\}_{\theta\in\Theta_{\sf N}}}{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbb{D}}\big[\Delta{\cal R}(\widehat F)\big] \ge c \cdot \frac{\xi^2}{{\sf N}}. \end{align*} In particular, the upper bound $O(\xi^2/{\sf N})$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:generalization:informal} is tight up to a constant.
nodes.statement_short: Some target family in the NTK RKHS forces every estimator to excess risk $\Omega(\xi^2/{\sf N})$.
assumptions: Fix a non-trivial subspace ${\cal H}^*\subseteq{\cal H}_K$ of the RKHS associated with the layer-wise NTKs
nodes.label: thm:lower_stat:informal

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Theorem B.2
nodes.statement: The argument is a Le Cam two-point reduction inside ${\cal H}^*$. Choose two targets $F_0^*, F_1^* \in {\cal H}^*$ with $\|F_0^*-F_1^*\|_{L^F({\cal X})}^2 = c_1\xi^2/{\sf N}$ and Gaussian-noise KL divergence $\frac{{\sf N}}{2\xi^2}\|F_0^*-F_1^*\|_{L^F}^2 \le \frac{1}{4}$. Le Cam's two-point lemma then gives $\inf_{\widehat F}\sup_j{\mathbb{E}}\Delta{\cal R}(\widehat F)\ge \frac{1}{8}\|F_0^*-F_1^*\|_{L^F}^2$. The full proof, which merely requires that ${\cal H}^*$ contain a non-zero direction, appears in Appendix~\ref{app_sub:lower_bounds}.
nodes.statement_short: Le Cam two-point reduction with two targets at squared distance $\Theta(\xi^2/{\sf N})$ and bounded KL.

nodes.name: Optimization-side lower bound (informal)
nodes.statement:
For any first-order optimization method ${\cal A}$ that, at each time, queries only the gradient $
abla_	heta {\cal L}(t,\mathbb{B}(t))$ within the parameter ball of Definition~ef{def:gd}, there exists an instance of the data distribution ${\cal D}$ and an initialization $	heta(0)$ such that the training loss after time $\sf T$ is lower-bounded by:  egin{align*} {\cal L}({\sf T}, \mathbb{D}) \ge c\cdot\exp(-C_{m opt}\cdot \omega\lambda_{\max} \cdot \varepsilon^2 {\sf T}) \cdot {\cal L}(0, \mathbb{D}), \end{align*} where $\lambda_{\max}:= \max_
u \lambda_{\max}(H_{(
u)}'(0))$ and $c, C_{m opt}>0$ are absolute constants. In particular, the exponent $-\Theta(\sqrt{\kappa}\,\xi^2{\sf C}/{\sf N}^7)$ (with $\kappa:=\lambda_{\max}/\lambda$) in the {\it Compute-Starved Stage} is tight up to constants and a $\sqrt{\kappa}$ factor in the exponent --- the unavoidable Nemirovski--Yudin condition-number gap; see Appendix~ef{app_sub:matching_precise}.
nodes.statement_short: No first-order method in the lazy ball beats $\exp(-C\omega\lambda_{\max}\varepsilon^2{\sf T})$ loss decay on some instance.
nodes.label: thm:lower_opt:informal

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Theorem B.3
nodes.statement: The training objective restricted to the parameter ball is a strongly convex quadratic in the linearization regime (kernel features are nearly fixed by Lemma~\ref{lem:perturbations:informal}). Standard first-order oracle complexity (Nemirovski--Yudin lower bounds for quadratic minimization, see e.g.~\citealp{nes03}) implies that no gradient-based method can decay the loss faster than $\exp(-\Theta(\sqrt{\lambda\lambda_{\max}})\,t)$ in continuous time, matching the discrete $((\sqrt\kappa-1)/(\sqrt\kappa+1))^{2T}$ bound after $T\to t/\eta$ with $\eta\to 0$. Translating to compute via ${\sf C}=O({\sf MTN})$ with ${\sf M}=\Theta({\sf N}^3)$ and incorporating the $1/\mathsf{N}$ factor in the rate (Remark~\ref{rem:n_in_rate}) recovers the $\exp(-\Theta(\sqrt{\kappa}\,\xi^2{\sf C}/{\sf N}^7))$ rate. The full argument is in Appendix~\ref{app_sub:lower_bounds}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a strongly convex quadratic and apply Nemirovski-Yudin oracle lower bounds, then translate to compute.

nodes.name: Cross-entropy vs. squared excess risk
nodes.statement: Cross-entropy after softmax shares its gradient form with squared loss in the logit space at the {\it Bregman / natural-gradient} level: with logits $z\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|}$, $y'={\rm softmax}(z)$, and one-hot $y\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|}$, $\partial_z {\cal L}_{\rm CE} = y'-y$ which is the gradient of the Bregman divergence $B_{\Phi^*}(y, y')$ where $\Phi^*$ is the log-partition; this matches the squared-loss gradient $z-y$ {\it only} in the well-specified, near-zero-excess regime ($y'\approx y$, e.g.~CE near $H(y)$). For typical LM training (CE $\sim 1.5$--$2$, far from $H(y)$), the two losses are not numerically identical even at the rate-exponent level, and our experiments are therefore meant to validate the {\it qualitative} predictions of Section~\ref{sec:scaling_law} (existence of the Stage~I/II transition; ${\sf N}^{1/2}$-noise breakdown of data scaling) rather than the exact exponents.
nodes.section: B.4 Cross-entropy vs.\ Squared Excess Risk
nodes.statement_short: Cross-entropy matches squared loss only near interpolation, so experiments validate the theory qualitatively.
nodes.label: rem:ce_l2

nodes.name: Transferring the N^{1/2}-noise breakdown to cross-entropy
nodes.statement:
The L$^2$ statement (Section~\ref{sub:potential_fails}) is: for noise variance $\xi^2(\mathsf{N})\propto \mathsf{N}$, the bound $O(\xi^2/\mathsf{N})\to O(1)$ saturates and data scaling fails. The CE analogue is the following token-level argument. Suppose a fraction $p_k$ of tokens in $D_k$ is corrupted by either (i) a fixed mask token (mask strategy) or (ii) a uniform random vocabulary token (random strategy). For strategy (ii), the corrupted tokens are unpredictable, and the irreducible CE on them is $\log V$ ($V$ = vocab size); the total CE then satisfies
\[
{\sf CE}(D_k) \ \ge\ p_k \cdot \log V + (1-p_k)\cdot {\sf CE}_{\rm clean}(D_k),
\]
so the {\it gap to clean} satisfies $\Delta {\sf CE}(D_k) \gtrsim p_k \cdot (\log V - {\sf CE}_{\rm clean})$, which under our schedule $p_k \propto \sqrt{\mathsf{N}(D_k)}$ grows as $\sqrt{\mathsf{N}}$. Once $\sqrt{\mathsf{N}}$ exceeds the rate at which ${\sf CE}_{\rm clean}$ improves (empirically a slow power of $\mathsf{N}$), the gap stalls and eventually grows --- exactly mirroring the L$^2$ saturation. For the mask strategy, $p_k\cdot \log V$ is replaced by $p_k\cdot {\sf KL}({\rm mask}\,\|\,{\sf next}|{\rm context})$ which is again $\Theta(p_k)$ at fixed mask-token statistics; the same scaling follows. Table~\ref{tab:noisy_training} reports the {\it stalling} portion of this prediction; the {\it growing} portion lies beyond the $0.5\to 2$M range and is observed in the extended Pythia sweep (Table~\ref{tab:noisy_extended}, Appendix~\ref{app_sub:wikitext_results}).
nodes.section: B.4 Cross-entropy vs.\ Squared Excess Risk
nodes.statement_short: Token corruption at rate $p_k\propto\sqrt{\sf N}$ makes the cross-entropy gap to clean training stall and grow, mirroring the $L^2$ saturation.

nodes.name: From masking probability to noise variance
nodes.statement:
The link between Table~\ref{tab:noisy_training} and the assumption $\xi({\sf N})\propto {\sf N}^{1/2}$ is more principled than the schedule label $\mathcal{M}_2$ alone suggests. Treat the embedding-space target as $Y_{\ell}^{\rm clean}$ and the corrupted target as $Y_\ell^{\rm clean}+ \Xi_\ell$ where $\Xi_\ell\in\mathbb{R}^d$ is non-zero only on the corrupted token positions. Conditional on the (fixed-pattern) corruption mask, $\Xi_\ell$ is the difference between the embedding of the {\it true} next token and the embedding of either (a) the dedicated mask token (strategy~$\mathcal{M}_*$ + mask-token) or (b) a uniform random token (strategy~$\mathcal{M}_*$ + all-token). Both differences are bounded by $2\max_v \|e_v\|_2 = O(1)$, and unconditional on the mask, ${\mathbb{E}}[\Xi_\ell]=0$ for the all-token variant (uniform vocabulary draws) and ${\mathbb{E}}[\Xi_\ell]=O(1)\cdot p_k$ for the mask-token variant (a fixed token offset weighted by $p_k$).
With per-token corruption probability $p_k\in[0,1]$, the per-position variance satisfies
\[
\mathrm{Var}[\Xi_\ell] \;=\; p_k\cdot O(1) \;-\; ({\mathbb{E}}[\Xi_\ell])^2 \;=\; \Theta(p_k)
\]
to leading order in $p_k$ for both strategies, so $\xi^2 = \Theta(p_k)$. Under schedule $\mathcal{M}_2 = \{0.10, 0.188, 0.231, 0.281\}$ on $\mathsf{N}\in\{0.5\text{M}, 1\text{M}, 1.5\text{M}, 2\text{M}\}$, the cumulative corruption rate scales as $p_k = 0.10\,\sqrt{\mathsf{N}/0.5\text{M}}$ (factor $2=\sqrt 4$ between endpoints), so $\xi^2 = \Theta(p_k)\propto \sqrt{\mathsf{N}}$, i.e.\ $\xi\propto \mathsf{N}^{1/4}$ {\it as a per-position embedding-space noise level} --- not the $\xi\propto {\sf N}^{1/2}$ of the headline theorem. The headline scaling $\xi\propto {\sf N}^{1/2}$ is what is required for the {\it variance} to grow linearly in ${\sf N}$ in the L$^2$ floor $\xi^2/{\sf N}$, which corresponds to $p_k\propto {\sf N}$ --- precisely what the extended schedule $\mathcal{M}_2^{\rm ext}$ of the Pythia case study realizes ($r_k=(2k-1)\cdot 0.05$, cumulative rate $0.05\,k$; Table~\ref{tab:noisy_extended}), subject to the cap $p_k\le 1$. The {\it qualitative direction} ($\xi^2$ growing with ${\sf N}$, gap-to-clean stalling) is what the table demonstrates; the exact exponent is therefore an upper bound on the achievable degradation rather than a literal numerical match. We highlight this distinction to keep the failure-mode claim within what the experiment actually establishes.
nodes.section: B.4 Cross-entropy vs.\ Squared Excess Risk
nodes.statement_short: Per-position embedding noise from corruption at rate $p_k$ has variance $\Theta(p_k)$, so $\xi^2=\Theta(p_k)$.

nodes.name: From continuous gradient flow to discrete SGD
nodes.statement:
Our convergence analysis is stated for continuous-time gradient flow, which is standard in the NTK literature \citep{jgh18, dzps19} and exposes the role of the kernel matrices $H_{(
u)}(t)$ most cleanly. The continuous-time picture extends to discrete SGD via the standard route taken in \citep{dzps19} (between their Section 3 and Section 4) and the prefix-NTK proof in \citep{lssy25} (Appendix H): given a small step size, a Taylor expansion of the per-step loss change isolates a {\it dominant term} of the form $\eta \cdot \langle
abla {\cal L}, H(t)
abla {\cal L}angle$ (matching the gradient-flow bound) plus {\it residual terms} of order $\eta^2$ that are controlled by over-parameterization (lazy learning) and shrink as the network width $m$ grows or the loss decreases. Provided the residual is bounded relative to the dominant term, the discrete bound matches the continuous one up to step-size factors. We focus on continuous time to keep the layered self-attention story clean and treat the discretization step as an orthogonal extension; full discrete analyses with adaptive optimizers (e.g.~AdamW) require additional bookkeeping but do not appear to change our two-stage qualitative conclusions.
nodes.section: B.5 From Continuous Gradient Flow to Discrete SGD
nodes.statement_short: A Taylor expansion of the per-step loss change gives the gradient-flow term plus $O(\eta^2)$ residuals controlled by over-parameterization.

nodes.name: What the bounds say in the rich regime
nodes.statement: For any feature-learning algorithm ${\cal A}_{\rm rich}$ that uses the same gradient information as our trajectory and is constrained to the lazy-training ball at the end of optimization, the upper bound of Theorem~\ref{thm:generalization:informal} continues to hold (since the ERM over the parameter ball is no smaller than what ${\cal A}_{\rm rich}$ achieves). Conversely, the optimization-side lower bound of Theorem~\ref{thm:lower_opt:informal} relies only on first-order oracle access and on the spectrum of the {\it initial} kernel $H_{(\nu)}'(0)$; it therefore applies verbatim to any first-order method, including feature-learning ones.
nodes.section: C.1 From Lazy to Rich: a Bridging Remark
nodes.statement_short: The ERM upper bound and the oracle lower bound still apply to feature-learning algorithms confined to the lazy ball.

nodes.name: Fully feature-learning analysis of multi-layer self-attention
nodes.statement: A fully feature-learning analysis at finite depth and finite width would require: (a) a kernel-{\it evolution} equation $\partial_t H_{(\nu)}(t) = \Phi(\theta(t), {\cal D})$ valid uniformly in $t$, (b) an explicit description of the long-time RKHS associated with $H_{(\nu)}(\infty)$, and (c) generalization bounds for the resulting time-dependent kernel regression problem. None of these are open-and-shut today for multi-layer self-attention; we therefore record the present analysis as a {\it baseline} that any rich-regime theorem must improve upon and refer the reader to \citep{boc+25, bap24, bcp24, ynh+22, ks24_nonlinear} for ongoing developments.
nodes.section: C.1 From Lazy to Rich: a Bridging Remark
nodes.statement_short: A rich-regime theory needs a kernel-evolution equation, the long-time RKHS, and generalization bounds for time-dependent kernel regression.

nodes.name: Origin of the xi^2 C / N^7 exponent
nodes.statement:
The exponent decomposes cleanly. The {\it generic} part is $\xi^2 \varepsilon^2 {\sf T}/\mathsf{N}$ (kernel-regression rate, with the $1/\mathsf{N}$ from the average-loss normalization; Remark~\ref{rem:n_in_rate}). Transformer-specific bookkeeping converts this into compute via three substitutions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(S1)] $\varepsilon = \xi/{\sf N}$ to balance approximation against the noise floor (Theorem~\ref{thm:scaling_law:informal}).
    \item[(S2)] ${\sf C} = {\sf MTN}$ with the lazy-regime width $m=\Omega({\sf N}^3)$ (T1 + T2 + T4 push the width condition up to ${\sf N}^3$, since the $nL\times nL$ kernel concentrates only at this width).
    \item[(S3)] ${\sf M}=\Theta(Nmd) = \Theta({\sf N}^3)$ on the boundary, giving ${\sf T} = {\sf C}/({\sf N}^4)$ and finally $\xi^2 \varepsilon^2 {\sf T}/\mathsf{N} = \xi^2/{\sf N}^2 \cdot {\sf C}/{\sf N}^4 \cdot 1/\mathsf{N} = \xi^2 {\sf C}/{\sf N}^7$.
\end{enumerate}
The exponent ${\sf N}^{-7}$ is therefore {\it part-generic, part-transformer}: the $\xi^2 \varepsilon^2 {\sf T}/\mathsf{N}$ factor is the generic kernel rate (the $1/\mathsf{N}$ being a normalization choice), but the substitution ${\sf N}^3 \to {\sf M}$ is a direct consequence of (T1)--(T4) and would change in shape (not just constants) if any of those ingredients were removed.
nodes.section: C.2 What is Transformer-Specific in the Two-Stage Law?
nodes.statement_short: The generic kernel rate $\xi^2\varepsilon^2{\sf T}/{\sf N}$ becomes $\xi^2{\sf C}/{\sf N}^7$ through $\varepsilon=\xi/{\sf N}$, ${\sf C}={\sf MTN}$ and ${\sf M}=\Theta({\sf N}^3)$.

nodes.name: Reducing the N^7 phase boundary
nodes.statement: Reducing ${\sf N}^7$ to a smaller polynomial would require {\it either} relaxing the lazy width condition (i.e.\ leaving the lazy ball, see Appendix~\ref{app_sub:lazy_to_rich}) or sharpening the kernel concentration argument for self-attention (an open problem).
nodes.section: C.2 What is Transformer-Specific in the Two-Stage Law?

nodes.name: Closing the lazy-ball restriction and the sqrt(kappa) gap
nodes.statement: We adopt ``matching up to $\mathrm{poly}(L,d,\kappa)$'' to make all three points visible at once; sharper rich-regime lower bounds (closing the lazy-ball restriction) {\it and} sharper algorithm-side analyses that close the $\sqrt{\kappa}$ gap (e.g.~accelerated gradient flow on the linearized loss) are open problems.
nodes.section: C.3 Precise Statement of the Matching Minimax Bounds

nodes.name: Two-regime piecewise law and elbow C*
nodes.statement:
Theorem~\ref{thm:scaling_law:informal} predicts a piecewise law of the form
\[
L({\sf C}) \approx \begin{cases} L_\infty + A e^{-\alpha_1 {\sf C}/{\sf N}^7} & {\sf C} \le {\sf C}^*({\sf N},\xi) \\ L_\infty + B {\sf C}^{-1/7} & {\sf C} \ge {\sf C}^*({\sf N},\xi) \end{cases}
\]
with elbow ${\sf C}^*\asymp {\sf N}^7 \log({\sf N}\cdot Ld/\xi^2)/\xi^2$.
nodes.section: C.4 Quantitative Diagnostics of the Compute--Data Phase Transition

nodes.name: Remark on the single matrix U
nodes.statement:
Remark on the single matrix $U_{(
u)}$: conventional implementations parameterize the attention logits with separate query and key projections $Q_{(
u)}, K_{(
u)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d 	imes d_{m head}}$ as $X Q_{(
u)} K_{(
u)}^	op X^	op$. Our formulation collapses this product into a single matrix $U_{(
u)} := Q_{(
u)} K_{(
u)}^	op \in \mathbb{R}^{d 	imes d}$, so the attention logit becomes $\kappa \cdot X U_{(
u)} X^	op$. This is an exact reparameterization of the bilinear form at the level of expressivity: any logit pattern realizable by $(Q_{(
u)}, K_{(
u)})$ with $d_{m head} = d$ is realizable by some $U_{(
u)}$, and vice versa. The reparameterization preserves the expressivity of the attention layer while collapsing two coupled matrices to one, which simplifies the kernel computation and the perturbation analysis. {\it Caveat:} gradient flow on $U_{(
u)}$ is {\it not} equivalent to gradient flow on $(Q_{(
u)}, K_{(
u)})$ — the latter has additional $Q$-$K$ coupling terms in the NTK and a different drift radius. Our analysis is therefore for gradient flow on $U_{(
u)}$ directly; results carry over to the $(Q,K)$ parameterization as a kernel upper bound (since the $(Q,K)$ tangent space is a quotient of the $U$ tangent space) but may differ in absolute constants. We discuss the implication for parameter counting in Appendix~ef{app:preli}.
nodes.section: C.5 The \texorpdfstring{$U_{(\nu)}$}{U} Parameterization and What Survives in the \texorpdfstring{$(Q,K)$}{(Q,K)} Form
nodes.statement_short: Collapsing $QK^\top$ into $U$ preserves expressivity but not the gradient flow; results transfer to $(Q,K)$ as kernel upper bounds.

nodes.name: Lazy-regime Chinchilla family C ~ N^{alpha+4}
nodes.statement: A natural family of corollaries is obtained by replacing the boundary ${\sf M}=\Theta({\sf N}^3)$ with ${\sf M}=\Theta({\sf N}^\alpha)$ for any $\alpha\ge 3$ (still satisfying Definition~\ref{def:gd}). Substituting into ${\sf C}={\sf MTN}$ with ${\sf T}\asymp {\sf N}^3\log({\sf N}\cdot Ld/\xi^2)/\xi^2$ at the Stage~I/II boundary yields the phase-transition family ${\sf C}\asymp {\sf N}^{\alpha+4}\log({\sf N}\cdot Ld/\xi^2)/\xi^2$ (recovering ${\sf N}^7$ at $\alpha=3$) — the lazy-regime analogue of the Chinchilla curve.
nodes.section: C.6 Empirical Interpretation, Limitations, and Future Directions
nodes.statement_short: With ${\sf M}=\Theta({\sf N}^\alpha)$, $\alpha\ge3$, the Stage I/II boundary becomes ${\sf C}\asymp{\sf N}^{\alpha+4}\log/\xi^2$.
assumptions: ${\sf M}=\Theta({\sf N}^\alpha)$ for any $\alpha\ge 3$ (still satisfying Definition~\ref{def:gd})

nodes.name: Sharper softmax-output bounds removing exp(Cd) width
nodes.statement: Both are loose for ``typical'' inputs but pessimistic in the worst case; sharpening them would require a finer concentration argument for the attention-output spectrum at initialization (open problem).
nodes.section: C.6 Empirical Interpretation, Limitations, and Future Directions

nodes.name: Network dimension d
nodes.statement: In this paper, we use integer $d$ to denote the dimension of networks.

nodes.name: Input length L
nodes.statement: We use $L$ to denote the input length in language models.

nodes.name: Derivative notation
nodes.statement: $\nabla_x f(x)$ and $\frac{\mathrm{d} f(x)}{\mathrm{d} x}$ are both means to take the derivative of $f(x)$ with $x$.

nodes.name: Vector norms
nodes.statement: We denote the $\ell_2$ norm as  $\|z\|_2:=( \sum_{i=1}^n z_i^2 )^{1/2}$, the $\ell_1$ norm as $\|z\|_1:=\sum_{i=1}^n |z_i| $, $\|z\|_0$ as the number of non-zero entries in $z$, $\| z \|_{\infty}$ as $\max_{i \in [n]} |z_i|$.

nodes.name: Inner product notation
nodes.statement: We use $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ to denote the inner product.

nodes.name: Expectation notation
nodes.statement: We use ${\mathbb{E}}[]$ to denote the expectation.

nodes.name: Probability notation
nodes.statement: We use $\Pr[]$ to denote the probability.

nodes.name: Row and column notation
nodes.statement: For a matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$, vector $A_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is the $i$-th row for $i \in [n]$ and vector $A_{*, j} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is the $j$-th column for $j \in [d]$.

nodes.name: Row notation for matrix-valued functions
nodes.statement: For a function $f: \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$, we use $f_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ to denote the $i$-th row of its output for $i \in [n]$ and us $f_{*, j} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ to denote the $j$-th column of its output for $j \in [d]$.

nodes.name: Weights and Initialization
nodes.statement:
The weights of the model are denoted as $	heta(t)$ where $t\ge 0$ is time. It contains the weights of each layer $	heta(t) = \{	heta_{(
u)}(t)\}_{
u=1}^N$, and $	heta_{(
u)} = \{ U_{(
u)}(t), W_{(
u)}(t), A_{(
u)} \}$. For each matrix:  egin{itemize} \item Each entry of $U_{(
u)}(0) \in \mathbb{R}^{d 	imes d}$ is initialized from the standard Gaussian distribution, formally, $U_{(
u), k_1, k_2}(0) \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ for any $k_1, k_2 \in [d]$. \item Each entry of $W_{(
u)}(0) \in \mathbb{R}^{d 	imes m}$ is initialized from the standard Gaussian distribution, formally, $w_{(
u), r, k}(0) \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ for any $r \in [m], k \in [d]$, where $w_{(
u), r}(0) \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is the $r$-th column of $W_{(
u)}(0)$. \item Each entry of $A_{(
u)}(0) \in \mathbb{R}^{m 	imes d}$ is initialized from a $\pm 1$ uniform distribution, formally, $a_{(
u), r, k}(0) $ $\sim {\sf Uniform}\{-1, +1\}$ for any $r \in [m], k \in [d]$, where $a_{(
u), r}(0) \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is the $r$-th row of $A_{(
u)}(0)$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Weights $\theta(t)$ per layer; $U(0),W(0)$ entries are standard Gaussian and $A(0)$ entries are uniform $\pm1$.

nodes.name: Data Distribution
nodes.statement: We denote $F^*: {\cal X} \to [C_1, C_2]^{L \times d}$ as the target function (with $F^*(X)$ bounded by fixed constants $C_1, C_2\in\mathbb{R}$). The input space ${\cal X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{L \times d}$ is a combination of $L$ $d$-dimensional balls where $\|X_\ell\|_2^2 = \Theta(1), \forall X\in {\cal X}, \ell \in [L]$. The data distribution is ${\cal D} = \{(X, F^*(X)+\Xi) : X\sim p_{\cal X},\, \Xi\sim p_\Xi\} \subset {\cal X} \times \mathbb{R}^{L\times d}$ where the noisy target $Y = F^*(X)+\Xi$ is unbounded in general. The random noise $\Xi \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times d}$ is centred by ${\bf 0}_{L \times d}$ and is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy $\xi^2$: ${\mathbb{E}}[\Xi] = {\bf 0}_{L\times d}$ and $\max_{\ell\in[L], k\in[d]} \|\Xi_{\ell,k}\|_{\psi_2}^2 \leq \xi^2$ (so ${\mathbb{E}}[\exp(t\Xi_{\ell,k})] \le \exp(t^2\xi^2/2)$). The Gaussian case $\Xi_{\ell,k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\xi^2)$ used in the Le Cam statistical lower bound (Theorem~\ref{thm:lower_stat}) is a special case. Only the noiseless target $F^*(X)$ is bounded; the noisy target $Y$ may take values outside $[C_1, C_2]^{L\times d}$, which is the natural setting under sub-Gaussian noise.
nodes.statement_short: Bounded noiseless target $F^*$ on unit-scale inputs plus centred sub-Gaussian noise with variance proxy $\xi^2$.

nodes.name: Original Dataset
nodes.statement: The original dataset is $\mathbb{D} = \{ (X_i, Y_i) \}_{i=1}^n \subset {\cal D}$, where $X_i, Y_i = F^*(X_i) + \Xi_i \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times d}$. For each data point $(X_i, Y_i), \forall i \in [n]$, it holds that: \begin{itemize} \item $\| X_{i, \ell} \|_2 = \Theta(1)$ for $\ell \in [L]$. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: def:D

nodes.statement:
Given an input matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{L 	imes d}$, the model function is given by ($\varepsilon > 0$ is the grokking coefficient):  egin{align*} F(X, 	heta(t)) := \varepsilon \cdot F_{(N)}(F_{(N-1)}( \cdots F_{(2)}(F_{(1)}(X + E, 	heta(t)), 	heta(t)) \cdots ), 	heta(t)). \end{align*} We list the original definition of each function as follows:  egin{itemize} \item  egin{align*} & ~ F_{(
u)}(X, 	heta(t)) :=  rac{\omega}{\sqrt{m}} {m ReLU}\left({m Softmax}\left( \kappa \cdot XU_{(
u)}(t)X^	op + M ight) XW_{(
u)}(t)ight)A_{(
u)} \end{align*} \item ${m Softmax}\left( A ight) := \mathrm{diag}(\exp(A){ f 1}_L)^{-1} \cdot \exp(A)\in \mathbb{R}^{L 	imes L}$ for $A \in \mathbb{R}^{L 	imes L}$. \item ${m ReLU}_{\ell, k}(X) := \max\{X_{\ell, k}, 0\}$ for any $\ell \in [L]$, $k \in [d]$, $X \in \mathbb{R}^{L 	imes d}$. \item $M_{\ell_1, \ell_2} :=  egin{cases} 0, & ~ \ell_1 \ge \ell_2 \ -\infty. & ~ \ell_1 < \ell_2 \end{cases},  orall \ell_1, \ell_2 \in [L]$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Full definition of the $N$-layer transformer with softmax, ReLU and the causal mask $M$.

nodes.statement:
We denote the special notations:  egin{itemize} \item We denote $w_{(
u), r}(t) \in \mathbb{R}^d$ as the $r$-th column of $W_{(
u)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d 	imes m}$ for $r\in [m]$, $
u \in [N]$. \item We denote $a_{(
u), r} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ as the $r$-th row of $A_{(
u)} \in \mathbb{R}^{m 	imes d}$ for $r\in [m]$, $
u \in [N]$. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Training objective (appendix)
nodes.statement: We define the training objective: \begin{align*} {\cal L}(t, \mathbb{D}) := {\mathbb{E}}_{(X, Y) \sim \mathbb{D}}[ \|F(X, \theta(t)) - Y \|_F^2 ] \end{align*}

nodes.name: Gaussian tail bound
nodes.statement: For a variable $x \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$, then with probability at least $1 - \delta$, we have: \begin{align*} |x| \leq C \sigma \sqrt{\log(1/\delta)} \end{align*}
assumptions: For a variable $x \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$
nodes.label: fac:gaussian_tail

nodes.name: 1-Lipschitz bound
nodes.statement: For an $1$-Lipschitz function $f(\cdot)$, we have: \begin{align*} | f(x) - f(y) | \leq | x - y |, \forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}^d \end{align*}
assumptions: For an $1$-Lipschitz function $f(\cdot)$
nodes.label: fac:lipschitz_1

nodes.name: Gaussian anti-concentration
nodes.statement: For a Gaussian variable $x \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 \cdot I_d )$ where $\sigma \in \mathbb{R}$, then for any $t > 0$, we have: \begin{align*} \Pr[x \leq t] \leq \frac{2t}{\sqrt{2\pi} \sigma } \end{align*}
assumptions: For a Gaussian variable $x \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 \cdot I_d )$ where $\sigma \in \mathbb{R}$
nodes.label: fac:anti_concen_gaussian

nodes.name: Gaussian inner product distribution
nodes.statement: For a Gaussian vector $w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 \cdot I_d )$ where $\sigma \in \mathbb{R}$, and a fixed vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, we have: \begin{align*} w^\top x \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 \|x\|_2^2 ) \end{align*}
assumptions: For a Gaussian vector $w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 \cdot I_d )$ where $\sigma \in \mathbb{R}$
a fixed vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$
nodes.label: fac:inner_product_gaussian

nodes.name: Eigenvalue perturbation bound
nodes.statement: For two matrices $H, \widetilde{H} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$, we have: \begin{align*} \lambda_{\min}( \widetilde{H} ) \ge \lambda_{\min} ( H ) - \| H - \widetilde{H} \|_F \end{align*}
assumptions: For two matrices $H, \widetilde{H} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$
nodes.label: fac:lambda_min_perturb

nodes.name: Lipschitz continuity of softmax
nodes.statement: The Lipchitz constant of the softmax function is bounded by $O(1)$, such that: \begin{align*} \| \langle \exp(x), {\bf 1}_L \rangle^{-1} \exp(x) - \langle \exp(y), {\bf 1}_L \rangle^{-1}\exp(y) \|_2 \leq O(1) \cdot \| x - y\|_2, \forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}^L. \end{align*}
conclusions: The Lipchitz constant of the softmax function is bounded by $O(1)$
nodes.label: fac:lipschitz_softmax

nodes.name: Minimum eigenvalue of a Kronecker product with identity
nodes.statement: For a matrix $H \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$, there is $\lambda_{\min}(H \otimes I_d) = \lambda_{\min}(H)$.
assumptions: For a matrix $H \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$
nodes.label: fac:lambda_min_krnocker

nodes.name: Hoeffding bound
nodes.statement: Let $X_1, \cdots , X_n$ denote $n$ independent bounded variables in $[a_i, b_i]$ for $a_i, b_i \in \mathbb{R}$. Let $X := \sum_{i=1}^n X_i$, then we have \begin{align*} \Pr[|X - {\mathbb{E}}[X]| \geq t] \leq 2\exp(- \frac{2t^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n (b_i -a_i)^2} ) \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $X_1, \cdots , X_n$ denote $n$ independent bounded variables in $[a_i, b_i]$ for $a_i, b_i \in \mathbb{R}$
nodes.label: lem:hoeffding

nodes.name: Markov's inequality
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a non-negative random variable and $a > 0$, then the probability that $X$ is at least $a$ is at most the expectation of $X$ divided by $a$: \begin{align*} \Pr[X \ge a] \leq \frac{{\mathbb{E}}[X]}{a} \end{align*}
assumptions: If $X$ is a non-negative random variable and $a > 0$
conclusions: the probability that $X$ is at least $a$ is at most the expectation of $X$ divided by $a$
nodes.label: lem:markov

nodes.name: Chernoff bound
nodes.statement: Let $X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i$, where $X_i = 1$ with probability $p_i$ and $X_i = 0$ with probability $1 - p_i$, and all $X_i$ are independent. Let $\mu = {\mathbb{E}}[X] = \sum_{i=1}^n p_i$. Then \begin{itemize} \item $\Pr[X \geq (1 + \delta)\mu] \leq \exp(-\delta^2\mu/3)$, $\forall \delta >0$; \item $\Pr[X \leq (1 - \delta)\mu] \leq \exp(-\delta^2\mu/1)$, $\forall 0 < \delta < 1$. \end{itemize}
assumptions: all $X_i$ are independent
nodes.label: lem:chernoff

nodes.name: Eigenvalue perturbation
nodes.statement: The stability of the PD property is ensured by $\lambda_{\min}(H') \ge \lambda_{\min}(H) - \| H - H' \|_F$ (Fact~\ref{fac:lambda_min_perturb}), since the perturbation $\| H - H' \|_F$ remains considerably small throughout training.
nodes.statement_short: Weyl-type bound keeps the kernel PD under small perturbation

nodes.name: Lazy regime
nodes.statement: The upper bound on the perturbation converges due to the increasing feed-forward layer width $m$ and the decreasing weight perturbation radius $R$, leading to the {\it Lazy Learning} regime. The complete proof of this lemma is stated in Appendix~\ref{app:proof_lperturbations}.
nodes.statement_short: Wide FFN and small drift radius make the perturbation vanish

nodes.name: Risk decomposition
nodes.statement: We decompose the excess risk $\Delta{\cal R}(F)$ into three terms: {\it i)} optimization risk ${\cal R}_{\rm optimization} := \| F(\cdot, \theta(t)) - F(\cdot, \theta(\infty)) \|_{L^F({\cal X})}^2$; {\it ii)} approximation risk ${\cal R}_{\rm approximation} :=  \big\| F(\cdot, \theta(\infty)) - {\rm arg}\inf_{F' \in {\cal F}_{\sf M, \infty, N}} \|F' - F^*\|_{L^F({\cal X})}^2 \big\|_{L^F({\cal X})}^2$; and {\it iii)} estimation risk ${\cal R}_{\rm estimation} := \inf_{F' \in {\cal F}_{\sf M, \infty, N}} \|F' - F^*\|_{L^F({\cal X})}^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Split excess risk into optimization, approximation and estimation terms
nodes.section: 6.1 General Scaling Law with Pattern Transition

nodes.name: Upper bounds
nodes.statement: The second and the third terms are already bounded in Theorem~\ref{thm:generalization:informal}, and the first term relates to the training loss; we thereby utilize Theorem~\ref{thm:convergence:informal} to finish the proof of the upper bounds.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the terms by the ERM and convergence theorems
nodes.section: 6.1 General Scaling Law with Pattern Transition

nodes.name: Lower bounds
nodes.statement: The matching lower bounds follow from a Le~Cam two-point reduction in the RKHS (Theorem~\ref{thm:lower_stat:informal}) and a first-order oracle complexity argument (Theorem~\ref{thm:lower_opt:informal}). The formal analysis is stated in Appendix~\ref{app_sub:scaling_law}, the lower bounds in Appendix~\ref{app_sub:lower_bounds}, and the precise sense of ``matching'' in Appendix~\ref{app_sub:matching_precise}.
nodes.statement_short: Lower bounds from Le Cam and oracle complexity
nodes.section: 6.1 General Scaling Law with Pattern Transition

nodes.name: FFN feature norm
nodes.statement: The post-activation FFN feature $\Lambda_{(\nu),i,\ell}^{\rm ffn}(t) := (\omega/\sqrt m)\,{\rm ReLU}(\mathrm{Softmax}(\cdots)$ $ X W_{(\nu)}(t)) \in \mathbb{R}^{1\times m}$ has bounded norm by Parts~3 and~5 of Lemma~\ref{lem:helpful_bounds}.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the post-activation FFN feature norm

nodes.name: Gradient envelope
nodes.statement: The gradient of the loss with respect to $A_{(\nu)}$ is therefore controlled by the same $\varepsilon\sqrt{{\cal L}(t,\mathbb{D})}$ envelope as that of $W_{(\nu)}$.
nodes.statement_short: The $A$-gradient obeys the same envelope as the $W$-gradient

nodes.name: Repeat bootstrap
nodes.statement: Repeating the bootstrapping step of Lemma~\ref{lem:perturbations:informal} with the additional kernel feature $\alpha_{(\nu),p}(t):= \Lambda^{\rm ffn}_{(\nu),p}(t)$ adds an $O(\omega)$ contribution to the kernel perturbation; the strengthened width condition is precisely what is needed for this contribution to remain $\le \omega\lambda/4$ at all times. The full proof appears in Appendix~\ref{app:proof_lperturbations}.
nodes.statement_short: Rerun the kernel-perturbation bootstrap with the extra feature

nodes.name: Le Cam reduction
nodes.statement: The argument is a Le Cam two-point reduction inside ${\cal H}^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Two-point reduction inside ${\cal H}^*$

nodes.name: Two targets
nodes.statement: Choose two targets $F_0^*, F_1^* \in {\cal H}^*$ with $\|F_0^*-F_1^*\|_{L^F({\cal X})}^2 = c_1\xi^2/{\sf N}$ and Gaussian-noise KL divergence $\frac{{\sf N}}{2\xi^2}\|F_0^*-F_1^*\|_{L^F}^2 \le \frac{1}{4}$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick two close targets with bounded KL divergence

nodes.name: Apply Le Cam
nodes.statement: Le Cam's two-point lemma then gives $\inf_{\widehat F}\sup_j{\mathbb{E}}\Delta{\cal R}(\widehat F)\ge \frac{1}{8}\|F_0^*-F_1^*\|_{L^F}^2$. The full proof, which merely requires that ${\cal H}^*$ contain a non-zero direction, appears in Appendix~\ref{app_sub:lower_bounds}.
nodes.statement_short: Le Cam's lemma gives the lower bound

nodes.name: Quadratic reduction
nodes.statement: The training objective restricted to the parameter ball is a strongly convex quadratic in the linearization regime (kernel features are nearly fixed by Lemma~\ref{lem:perturbations:informal}).
nodes.statement_short: In the lazy regime the objective is a strongly convex quadratic

nodes.name: Oracle lower bound
nodes.statement: Standard first-order oracle complexity (Nemirovski--Yudin lower bounds for quadratic minimization, see e.g.~\citealp{nes03}) implies that no gradient-based method can decay the loss faster than $\exp(-\Theta(\sqrt{\lambda\lambda_{\max}})\,t)$ in continuous time, matching the discrete $((\sqrt\kappa-1)/(\sqrt\kappa+1))^{2T}$ bound after $T\to t/\eta$ with $\eta\to 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Nemirovski-Yudin first-order lower bounds

nodes.name: Translate to compute
nodes.statement: Translating to compute via ${\sf C}=O({\sf MTN})$ with ${\sf M}=\Theta({\sf N}^3)$ and incorporating the $1/\mathsf{N}$ factor in the rate (Remark~\ref{rem:n_in_rate}) recovers the $\exp(-\Theta(\sqrt{\kappa}\,\xi^2{\sf C}/{\sf N}^7))$ rate. The full argument is in Appendix~\ref{app_sub:lower_bounds}.
nodes.statement_short: Convert the rate into compute units

nodes.name: Rearranged Dataset
nodes.statement: Given the origin dataset $\mathbb{D} = \{X_i, Y_i\}_{i=1}^n \subset \mathbb{R}^{L \times d} \times \mathbb{R}^{L \times d }$. The rearranged dataset is $\mathbb{D}_{\rm rearrange} = \{ (X_{i, \le \ell} + E_{\leq \ell}, Y_{i, \ell}) \}_{(i, \ell)=(1, 1)}^{(n, L)}$, where $X_{i, \le \ell}+ E_{\leq \ell} \in \mathbb{R}^{\ell \times d}$ and $Y_{i, \ell} \in \mathbb{R}^d$.

nodes.statement_short: Stacks per-token outputs and targets into $nL\times d$ matrices and lists the per-layer hidden states, attention scores, outputs and FFN terms.

nodes.name: Compact form of the training loss
nodes.statement: We have: \begin{align*} {\cal L}(t, \mathbb{D}) = \frac{1}{n} \| {\sf F}(t) - {\sf Y}\|_F^2 \end{align*}
also_stated_at: Therefore, we derive ${\cal L}(t, \mathbb{D}) = \frac{1}{n} \| {\sf F}(t) - {\sf Y}\|_F^2$ (See Lemma~\ref{lem:compact_form_transform}).
nodes.label: lem:compact_form_transform

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma F.3
nodes.statement: Since the decoder-only property of the model function, we have: \begin{align*} F_{(i-1)L+\ell}(t) = F_{\ell}(X_i, \theta(t)), \forall (X_i, Y_i) \in \mathbb{D}, i \in [n], \ell \in [L]. \end{align*} We then separate each token vector with: \begin{align*} {\cal L}(t, \mathbb{D}) = & ~ {\mathbb{E}}_{(X, Y) \sim \mathbb{D}}[ \|F(X, \theta(t)) - Y \|_F^2 ] \\ = & ~ \frac{1}{n} \sum_{(X, Y) \in \mathbb{D}} \|F(X, \theta(t)) - Y \|_F^2 \\ = & ~ \frac{1}{n} \sum_{(X, Y) \in \mathbb{D}} \sum_{\ell=1}^L \| F_{\ell}(X, \theta(t)) - Y_\ell\|_2^2 \\ = & ~ \frac{1}{n} \| {\sf F}(t) - {\sf Y}\|_F^2, \end{align*} where the first three steps follow from simple algebra, and the last step follows from the definitions of ${\sf F}$ and ${\sf Y}$.
nodes.statement_short: Decoder-only causality lets each token row be separated; sum the per-token squared errors.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma F.4
nodes.statement:
We derive each part by explicit application of the multivariable chain rule. We use the shorthand $p = (i-1)L+\ell$ with $i \in [n]$, $\ell \in [L]$ throughout. { f Part 1: Gradient with respect to $U_{(
u)}(t)$.} The dependence chain is  egin{align*} {\cal L}(t,\mathbb{D}) \xleftarrow{	ext{layer-$
u$ output}} \mu_{(
u),p}(t) \xleftarrow{	ext{FFN}} o_{(
u),p}(t) \xleftarrow{	ext{attention output}} \sigma_{(
u),p}(t) & ~ \xleftarrow{	ext{softmax}}  ig[\Lambda_{(
u-1),i}(t) U_{(
u)}(t) \Lambda_{(
u-1),i,\ell}(t) ig] \ & ~ \xleftarrow{} U_{(
u)}(t). \end{align*} Apply the chain rule layer by layer. For the softmax step, with logits $z_{p,\ell'} := \Lambda_{(
u-1),i,\ell'}(t)^	op U_{(
u)}(t) \Lambda_{(
u-1),i,\ell}(t)$ (causal $\ell'\le \ell$) and $\sigma_{(
u),p}(t) = {m softmax}(z_p+M_{\ell})$, the standard softmax-Jacobian identity gives:  egin{align*}  rac{\mathrm{d} \sigma_{(
u),p,\ell'}(t)}{\mathrm{d} z_{p,\ell''}} =  ig[\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{(
u),p}(t)) - \sigma_{(
u),p}(t)\sigma_{(
u),p}(t)^	op ig]_{\ell',\ell''}. \end{align*} The Kronecker identity $\mathrm{d} z_{p,\ell'}/\mathrm{d} \mathrm{vec}(U_{(
u)}(t)) =  ig(\Lambda_{(
u-1),i,\ell}(t) \otimes \Lambda_{(
u-1),i,\ell'}(t) ig)^	op$, combined with the chain $\sigma	o o	o \mu 	o {\cal L}$, then yields:  egin{align*}  rac{\mathrm{d}{\cal L}(t,\mathbb{D})}{\mathrm{d} \mathrm{vec}(U_{(
u)}(t))} &= \sum_{p\in[nL]}  rac{\mathrm{d} {\cal L}}{\mathrm{d} \mu_{(
u),p}(t)}^	op rac{\mathrm{d} \mu_{(
u),p}(t)}{\mathrm{d} o_{(
u),p}(t)} rac{\mathrm{d} o_{(
u),p}(t)}{\mathrm{d} \sigma_{(
u),p}(t)} rac{\mathrm{d} \sigma_{(
u),p}(t)}{\mathrm{d} z_p} rac{\mathrm{d} z_p}{\mathrm{d} \mathrm{vec}(U_{(
u)}(t))}. \end{align*} Substituting (i) $\mathrm{d}\mu_{(
u),p}/\mathrm{d} o_{(
u),p} =  rac{\omega}{\sqrt m}\sum_r a_{(
u),r}^	op w_{(
u),r}(t)\,\mathbb{I}\{w_{(
u),r}(t)^	op o_{(
u),p}(t)>0\}$ from the ReLU derivative, (ii) $\mathrm{d} o_{(
u),p}/\mathrm{d} \sigma_{(
u),p} = \Lambda_{(
u-1),i}(t)^	op$, and (iii) the softmax Jacobian above, we obtain Part~1 after combining factors:  egin{align*}  rac{\mathrm{d}{\cal L}(t,\mathbb{D})}{\mathrm{d}\mathrm{vec}(U_{(
u)}(t))} = &~  rac{\omega\kappa}{\sqrt{m}}\sum_{p=1}^{nL} ig(\Lambda_{(
u-1),i,\ell}(t)\otimes \Lambda_{(
u-1),i}(t) ig)^	op \cdot ig(\mathrm{diag}\sigma_{(
u),p}(t)-\sigma_{(
u),p}(t)\sigma_{(
u),p}(t)^	op ig)\Lambda_{(
u-1),i}(t)\ \cdot &~ \sum_{r}\!\Big\langle	frac{\mathrm{d}{\cal L}}{\mathrm{d}\mu_{(
u),p}(t)},a_{(
u),r}\Bigangle w_{(
u),r}(t)\mathbb{I}\{\cdot\}. \end{align*} { f Part 2: Gradient with respect to $w_{(
u),r}(t)$.} Since $w_{(
u),r}(t)$ enters the model only through the ReLU activation $\phi(\langle w_{(
u),r}(t), o_{(
u),p}(t)angle)$ in the layer-$
u$ FFN, the chain rule gives:  egin{align*}  rac{\mathrm{d}{\cal L}(t,\mathbb{D})}{\mathrm{d} w_{(
u),r}(t)} = \sum_{p=1}^{nL} rac{\mathrm{d}{\cal L}}{\mathrm{d}\mu_{(
u),p}(t)}^	op\cdot  rac{\mathrm{d} \mu_{(
u),p}(t)}{\mathrm{d} w_{(
u),r}(t)}. \end{align*} The $r$-th component of $\mu_{(
u),p}(t)$ is $ rac{\omega}{\sqrt m} a_{(
u),r}\phi(\langle w_{(
u),r}(t), o_{(
u),p}(t)angle)$, whose derivative with respect to $w_{(
u),r}(t)$ equals $ rac{\omega}{\sqrt m} a_{(
u),r}\, o_{(
u),p}(t)\,\mathbb{I}\{w_{(
u),r}(t)^	op o_{(
u),p}(t)>0\}$ by the ReLU sub-gradient. Substituting yields Part~2. { f Part 3: Gradient with respect to $\mu_{(
u),p}(t)$ via back-propagation.} The model output ${\sf F}_p(t) = \varepsilon\sum_{
u'=0}^N \mu_{(
u'),p}(t)$ depends on $\mu_{(
u),p}(t)$ both directly (the additive term in the residual sum) and indirectly through its effect on $\mu_{(
u+1),p}(t),\dots,\mu_{(N),p}(t)$ in subsequent layers. The direct contribution to $\mathrm{d} {\cal L}/\mathrm{d} \mu_{(
u),p}(t)$ is $ rac{2\varepsilon}{n}({\sf F}_p(t)-{\sf Y}_p)$ from the squared-loss derivative. The indirect contribution arises because $\mu_{(
u),p}(t)$ enters the layer-$(
u+1)$ hidden state as part of $\Lambda_{(
u),i,\ell}(t) = \Lambda_{(
u-1),i,\ell}(t) + \mu_{(
u),p}(t)$, which feeds into the attention logits $z_{p,\ell'}$ at layer $
u+1$. The dependence is captured by the $G$-factor:  egin{align*} G_{(
u),p}(t) :=  rac{\mathrm{d} \mu_{(
u+1),p}(t)}{\mathrm{d} \mu_{(
u),p}(t)}. \end{align*} Decomposing $\mathrm{d}\mu_{(
u+1),p}/\mathrm{d}\mu_{(
u),p}$ into (i) the contribution through $\sigma_{(
u+1),p}(t)$ (attention) and (ii) the contribution through $o_{(
u+1),p}(t)$ (the next attention output), and substituting the softmax Jacobian and ReLU sub-gradient, we obtain the explicit form:  egin{align*} G_{(
u),p}(t) &=  rac{\omega}{\sqrt m}\Big(\sigma_{(
u),p,\ell}(t) I_d + \kappa U_{(
u)}(t)\Lambda_{(
u-1),i}(t)^	op\mathrm{diag}({ f 1}_n-	frac{1}{2}e_\ell) ig(\mathrm{diag}\sigma_{(
u),p}(t)-\sigma_{(
u),p}(t)\sigma_{(
u),p}(t)^	op ig)\Lambda_{(
u-1),i}(t)\Big) \ &\quad\cdot \sum_{r\in[m]}\Big\langle	frac{\mathrm{d}{\cal L}}{\mathrm{d}\mu_{(
u+1),p}(t)},a_{(
u),r}\Bigangle w_{(
u),r}(t)\,\mathbb{I}\{o_{(
u),p}(t)^	op w_{(
u),r}(t)>0\}. \end{align*} The boundary condition $G_{(N),p}(t)={ f 0}_d$ holds because there is no layer beyond $N$. Combining the direct and indirect terms:  egin{align*}  rac{\mathrm{d}{\cal L}(t,\mathbb{D})}{\mathrm{d} \mu_{(
u),p}(t)} =  rac{2\varepsilon}{n} ig(I_d + \mathrm{diag}(G_{(
u),p}(t)) ig) ig({\sf F}_p(t) - {\sf Y}_p ig), \end{align*} which is Part~3.
nodes.statement_short: Multivariable chain rule through softmax Jacobian, ReLU sub-gradient and the residual back-propagation factor $G$.

nodes.name: Learning dynamics
nodes.statement:
The learning dynamics of the multi-layer transformer Equation~\eqref{eq:F} is given by:  egin{align*} {\mathbb{E}}[ rac{\mathrm{d} }{\mathrm{d} t}{\cal L}(t, \mathbb{D})] = - \sum_{
u \in [N]} {\underbrace{\mathrm{vec}\left( rac{\mathrm{d} }{\mathrm{d} \mu_{(
u)}(t)}{\cal L}(t, \mathbb{D}) ight)^	op}_{1 	imes nLd}} \cdot \underbrace{\left( H_{(
u)}(t) \otimes I_d ight)}_{nLd 	imes nLd} \cdot \underbrace{\mathrm{vec}\left( rac{\mathrm{d} }{\mathrm{d} \mu_{(
u)}(t)}{\cal L}(t, \mathbb{D}) ight)}_{nLd 	imes 1} \end{align*} where $\mu_{(
u)}(t)$ is an $nL 	imes d$ matrix, $\mu_{(
u), p}(t)$ is the $(p	ext{ mod } L)$-th row of the $
u$-th layer output for input matrix $X_{\lfloor p / L floor}$ for any $p \in [nL]$ and $
u \in [N]$.
nodes.statement_short: Expected loss derivative equals minus the sum over layers of hidden-state-gradient quadratic forms in $H_{(\nu)}\otimes I_d$.
